title: Of cripples
hookLine: he warns against being too sure, especially when condemning people as witches (Essays 3.11)

cards: They say. I think. Montaigne writes that he loves these little words, the ones that soften a sentence and take the swagger out of it.
An odd thing to love; they don't sound brave. The essay where he says it, in book three, carries an old English title, Of cripples, taken from a passage near its end about a common saying.
But much of it is about something far heavier: what happens when people are too sure, and someone else pays for it.

teach.b: First, how stories grow. People would rather explain a strange event than check whether it happened, Montaigne notices. They skip past the facts and argue carefully about the causes.
And each time a tale is passed along, it grows a little, because the teller wants to convince. Second, the witches. In his time, people accused of witchcraft were put on trial and burned.
Montaigne says he was shown some accused people himself, and his judgment was gentle and blunt at once: they seemed more in need of medicine than of execution.

teach.h: A HIGH PRICE ON OUR GUESSES.
teach.b: Then the sentence this essay is remembered for, roughly: it is putting a very high price on our guesses to roast a person alive because of them. Third, the little words again. Now perhaps and I think sound different.
They aren't weakness; they're a brake. He'd like the young to be taught to answer with words like: what does that mean? I don't understand it.
It could be. Better to sound like a learner than certain too soon. Fourth, closer to home.

Few of us will sit in judgment at a trial, but we judge all the time: a neighbor's motive, a stranger's character, a relative's choices, often from a story that grew as it passed along. His question still works.
Sure enough for what it would cost them if I'm wrong?

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of cripples often remember it for its warning against condemning people on uncertain grounds, and for his love of softening words like perhaps and I think.

a list of cures he tried for his own bad leg
an essay on caring for people who cannot walk

s: Montaigne says people check the facts before explaining a strange event
he says they skip the facts and argue carefully about the causes.

games.q: you're Montaigne, and you've been shown people accused of witchcraft. what do you conclude?
o: the evidence is clear; let the trial go on.
they seem to need medicine more than execution.
say nothing; it's not your business.
games.why: he judged them more in need of medicine, and said it puts a very high price on our guesses to burn a person for them.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've judged hard lately, and notice the verdict already written in your head. Gently put one of Montaigne's little words in front of it: perhaps, they say, I think.
You don't have to change your mind; just hold it a little more loosely.

wordCard.voice: Of cripples. Montaigne's essay against being too sure, especially when someone else will pay for our certainty. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French title for Essays 3.11, Of cripples, meaning of the lame.

carryVoice: Your line: not so sure. Perhaps is a small word, and it can carry a lot of mercy. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays 3.11, Of cripples (words that soften: perhaps, in some sort, some, they say, I think; people pass over facts and examine causes; stories grow in the telling; accused witches who seemed to need medicine; a high price on conjectures to roast a man alive)
